covers: Opening: a member on a GLP-1 medication steps on the scale and the number drops again. The app logs the loss, but that number can't show what made up the change: fat, lean mass, or fluid.

What FitXpress is, shown on real scan footage: not an app members download; it runs inside the fitness app. Two phone photos (front and side), pose and framing checked in real time, structured results back in under 45 seconds: 80+ body measurements, a 3D model, and body composition estimates (body fat percentage, fat mass, lean mass).

Two product views the video shows: the app can show two scans side by side, as 3D models and measurements; and a member can set a goal weight and see a 3D model of their body at that weight, «a goal to work toward, not a forecast of treatment results».

The research: the 2024 Neeland, Linge and Birkenfeld review (both ranges), lean mass is not muscle, and the 2025 joint advisory (strength training alongside adequate protein); a fitness app supports the training part, the rest stays with nutrition and medical care.

A progress view in four rows: weight trend, body measurements, fat and lean mass estimates (labeled as estimates, lean mass is not muscle mass), and the training record the app already keeps; what to do when weight falls but the waist doesn't.
Comparable check-ins: a baseline at onboarding or the start of a strength program, check-ins at set points, the same clothing, time of day and setting.
What the numbers cover and what they don't, and a pilot with five signals: capture completion and retakes, valid baseline and follow-up scans, on-schedule check-ins, progress-view opens.
rules: The post's job is to get the right reader (product and growth leads at fitness and coaching apps whose members are on GLP-1 treatment) to watch the video. Name what they will see in it, concretely; never summarise the whole video so that watching becomes pointless.

The link in every post is the YouTube URL above. Instagram captions don't carry clickable links: point to the link in bio there. The article URL may appear only as a second, optional link on LinkedIn or Facebook.

No accuracy figures in any post (Vadim, 2026-11-18: accuracy numbers are hard-out for social). The video's 4:15 chapter may be named as «what the numbers cover and what they don't», without the numbers.
Goal visualization: always as a goal the member sets and works toward, never as a prediction, forecast or expected treatment result.
Body Progress: «the app can show two scans side by side». Never «FitXpress tracks members / patients over time».

Do not repeat the article pack's entry points (table below): those posts went out 2026-11-06 about the same article. The new thing here is the video: real scan footage, the product views, six minutes.
No people named from the video footage and no customer names. No clinical outcome claims: nothing about preventing muscle loss or better results.
